renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: collapse_vs_length
  title: Collapse rate against retained length
  description: |-
    Each point is one AdapterRemoval report, usually a lane or a library: the mean length of its retained sequences against the share of read pairs merged into a single sequence, sized by the sequences retained. It answers whether the insert sizes of a library are short enough for mates to overlap.
    How to read: short fragments make the mates overlap, so a high collapse rate goes with a short retained length. That is the expected shape of an ancient or degraded DNA library. A low collapse rate with long retained sequences means the inserts are longer than the reads and the mates cannot merge.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median collapse rate of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of AdapterRemoval.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    x_title: Average retained length (bp)
    y_title: Share of pairs collapsed
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: average_retained_length
    y: collapse_rate
    label: sample
    color: sample
    size: retained_reads

- component: figure
  title: Sequences retained per report
  description: |-
    Each bar is one AdapterRemoval report: the number of sequences it wrote out, which is the input of the mapper. It answers how much data each report contributes after trimming and collapsing.
    How to read: reports of one library type should be of similar size. A very short bar is a report that lost most of its reads to discarding, so check its discard rate before pooling it.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median number of sequences retained per report of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of AdapterRemoval.
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: retained_reads
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Report
      retained_reads: Sequences retained
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: retained_reads

- component: card
  title: Read pairs processed
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of read pairs given to AdapterRemoval across the reports, and the strip steps down to the pairs whose mates overlapped and the pairs merged into one sequence. It answers how much of the input survives each step.
    How to read: a short step from overlapping to collapsed means most overlapping pairs were merged. A large drop from input to overlapping means long inserts, which is normal for modern DNA and unusual for ancient DNA.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  column: total_read_pairs
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: attrition
  attrition_cols:
  - well_aligned_read_pairs
  - collapsed_pairs
  caption: pairs, from input to overlapping to collapsed

- component: card
  title: Collapse rate
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across reports of the share of read pairs merged into a single sequence, and the box shows the spread. It answers how often the mates overlap enough to merge.
    How to read: a high share is the expected shape of an ancient or degraded library, with short fragments. A low share on such a library suggests modern DNA or long inserts. A report far from the box deserves a look at its library preparation.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  column: collapse_rate
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Retained length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across reports of the mean length of a retained sequence, in base pairs, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the sequences handed to the mapper are.
    How to read: short sequences map ambiguously and long ones map better. A report well below its peers may have been over-trimmed or be a degraded library.
  column: average_retained_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Discard rate
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across reports of the share of reads dropped on quality or length, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much data trimming throws away.
    How to read: a low share means the library trims cleanly. A report far above its peers has many reads too short or too poor to keep, which points to adapter dimers or degraded input.
    Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  column: discard_rate
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Sequences retained
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of sequences written out across the reports, and the histogram counts the reports by how many each retained. It answers how much data is left for mapping and how evenly the reports contribute.
    How to read: a tight pile means evenly sized reports. A long tail of small reports holds the lanes or libraries that lost most of their reads.
  column: retained_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: reports, by sequences retained

- component: table
  title: Trimming and collapsing statistics
  description: |-
    One row is one AdapterRemoval report, with its read counts at each step, retained length, collapse rate and discard rate. It gives the exact values behind the tiles and answers which reports lose or merge the most reads.
    How to read: sort by discard rate to find the reports that lose the most reads, then by collapse rate to see how many pairs were merged. The counts balance, so pairs in, mates merged and reads discarded add up to the sequences retained. It complements the collapse rate and discard rate tiles.
